result:
I keep thinking about the word "still." It's a small word that refuses to settle on one meaning. Still as in motionless: a pond with no wind on it. Still as in continuing: she is still here. Still as in the apparatus that patiently coaxes spirit out of fermented mash, drop by drop. Still as a photograph, a single frame lifted out of the river of a film.

What strikes me is how these meanings lean on each other. To be still, in the sense of unmoving, is often how something manages to still be, in the sense of persisting. The stone endures because it does not hurry. The distiller's still works precisely because it holds heat steady and lets time do the rest. A still image outlasts the scene it captured because it stopped.

There is also the quieting sense: to still a crying child, to still one's own racing thoughts. This is the hardest version. Stillness of water is easy; the pond doesn't have to try. Stillness of a mind is a kind of labor that looks, from outside, like nothing at all.

I wonder if the word survived so many meanings because they all share a feeling of pressure released. Something that was straining stops straining, and in that stopping, something clarifies. The sediment sinks. The vapor separates. The frame comes into focus.

So: still. Motionless, ongoing, refining, captured, calmed. A whole philosophy folded into five letters, waiting quietly, still.
